newsitem.title: INDIA: India United Front says willing to replace chief.
newsitem.headline: India United Front says willing to replace chief.

text.p: India's 15-party United Front coalition said on Sunday it might consider a demand by the rival Congress party to replace its leader, defeated Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda, and avert fresh elections.
Deve Gowda offered to step down from the leadership of United Front at the two-hour long meeting, the United News of India (UNI) reported.

"I am not saying that a change in leadership is ruled out," a senior United Front official, who asked not to be named, told reporters after a meeting of the coalition's decision-making Steering Committee.
"Till yesterday, we were saying that a change in leadership is not negotiable," he said.

Deve Gowda told the Steering Commitee that he would obey its decisions, United Front spokesman Jaipal Reddy told reporters, adding that the United Front would take a final decision on the leadership issue on April 17.

Deve Gowda resigned on Friday after losing a vote of confidence in the lower house of parliament but agreed to remain as caretaker prime minister. The United Front earlier said there was no question of replacing him as coalition leader.

Its sudden reversal came after leaders of four key regional parties, constituents in the United Front, held talks before the Steering Committee meeting and made clear that they did not want mid-term elections.
Reddy said the four parties -- two from Tamil Nadu state, one from Andhra Pradesh and the fourth from Assam -- "expressed the view that elections must be avoided."
Referring to the Steering Committee, he added: "The general view was elections should be avoided."
Congress, which precipitated Deve Gowda's defeat by withdrawing its support, has said it will consider helping the United Front to form a new government provided the alliance dropped its leader.
The senior United Front official was asked how the United Front and Congress could reach common ground to set up a new government.
He said the decision-making Congress Working Committee, set to meet on Monday, would have to withdraw a written claim, given last month to President Shankar Dayal Sharma, to form a government.
"The CWC must make the formal offer. They must convey their latest decision to the president, which means a reversal of the earlier decision," he said.
Congress parliamentary deputy and former minister Rajesh Pilot said he was optimistic that the two groups would sink their differences and hammer out a compromise very soon.

"I am very sure both the groups, having the national interest in mind, are ready to sacrifice individuals...in the political interest. I think we can find a solution even as early as the next two or three days," Pilot told Reuters Television.
